description_ru: Во время грозы в театре гаснет свет, и многолетняя дублёрша наконец получает свой шанс, хотя выходит на сцену лишь голосом из темноты.
text:
Marguerite Aubrey had been the understudy for Dame Constance Pryor for nineteen years, which was long enough to learn two things. The first was that a good understudy is a kind of ghost, present at every rehearsal and absent from every poster. The second was that the Dame, who was robust, bad-tempered and immortal, would never once miss a performance.

She had learned the role of Queen Margaret so thoroughly that she dreamed it in a voice that was not her own. Each evening she stood in the wings of the Alhambra Theatre with a flask of lukewarm tea, mouthing the lines a half-second behind the star, and each evening the Dame swept off to applause that was not meant for her. Marguerite did not resent it, or so she told herself. Resentment, she had decided long ago, was a luxury for people with options. Her sister in Leeds sent a postcard every Christmas asking when she would be given a proper part, and every year Marguerite replied that the part was proper enough, it merely belonged to someone else.

On the last Saturday of the run, the storm arrived. It had been rumbling over the river since the afternoon, and by the interval the rain was hammering the roof like a hundred impatient fists. At twenty to nine, in the middle of the third act, the lights went out.

There was a moment of perfect silence, followed by the kind of nervous laughter that only a dark auditorium can produce. The stage manager hissed instructions into his headset. The generator, he announced, would take twenty minutes to start. The Dame, standing blind in the middle of the stage, said something unprintable and sat down on the throne.

"We'll have to refund the house," the producer whispered to Marguerite, who had appeared beside him as if summoned. "Eight hundred people. They'll be furious." "They're not furious yet," said Marguerite. "They're curious. That's a different animal." She was surprised to hear herself say it. Something odd was happening in her chest, a loosening, as if a corset she had worn for nineteen years had quietly given way. She walked to the edge of the wings, took the stage manager's torch, and looked at the Dame. The old woman was tired, her hands were trembling, and the tremor had nothing to do with the dark.

"Constance," Marguerite said softly. "Do you want to finish it without light?" "Finish it? My dear girl, the audience can't see a thing." "Then they'll listen. Nobody has listened to this play properly since it was written."

The Dame stared at her for a long moment, with an expression Marguerite had never seen before, a sort of reluctant respect. Then she stood, crossed the stage with a rustle of heavy silk, and said, in the voice that had filled this theatre for four decades, "Ladies and gentlemen, a small technical difficulty. We shall continue regardless. I suggest you close your eyes. Most of you have seen worse productions with them open."

The laughter that followed was warm, almost grateful. The actors, one by one, found their positions by memory and touch. For the first time in the history of the production, nobody was performing for the front row. Without the lighting, the costumes or the elaborate scenery, there was only language, passing from voice to voice through the darkness like a lantern. A child in the circle asked in a carrying whisper whether the play was supposed to be like this, and her mother answered, equally loudly, that she hoped so, because it was the best thing she had ever heard.

In the final scene, Queen Margaret has to deliver a long speech of defeat. Halfway through it, the Dame faltered. It was not a lapse of memory; it was exhaustion, the plain physical kind that no technique can hide. The silence stretched. Somewhere in the stalls, a man coughed.

From the wings, scarcely louder than breathing, Marguerite supplied the next line. It was not a prompt. A prompt is a mechanical thing, a cue thrown across the gap. This was something else, the same words in the same cadence, but with a heartbeat behind them. The Dame heard it, drew a long breath, and picked up the speech exactly where it had fallen. By the end, the two voices had somehow become one, each carrying the other through the difficult passages, and when the final line was spoken the dark seemed to hold it for a moment before releasing it.

Then the generator caught, and the lights came up on a stage with nobody on it but the Dame, who stood perfectly still with tears on her face, and an audience that was already on its feet.

Afterwards, in the corridor outside the dressing rooms, the Dame found her sitting on a laundry basket. "You prompted me," she said. "I'm sorry. It was unforgivable."

"It was," said the Dame. "I have been furious for the past ten minutes, and I intend to remain so until the weekend." She paused, adjusting a heavy ring. "I have also decided to retire in the spring. Don't make that face, you'll get wrinkles. They will ask you to play Margaret, you realise, if only because they cannot find anybody else who knows the part, and for once you will not say yes immediately. You will make them wait, and you will insist on being paid properly." "And if I forget the lines?" "Marguerite," said the Dame, with something that was almost tenderness, "you have never forgotten a line in your life. It's the only thing about you that has ever frightened me.

focus_sounds.tip_ru: Ударение: ˈunderstudy, auditoˈrium (второстепенное на au-), unforˈgivable. В длинных словах чётко выделяйте один главный слог.
Для «th» в служебных словах (the, that, there) язык между зубами, звук звонкий, без «з».
Тёмное «l» в конце слога: язык поднят к альвеолам, а спинка опущена, как нечто среднее между «л» и «у».
Тянуть слова вместе: picked_up звучит как «пикт-ап».

questions.question: How long had Marguerite been the understudy?
What happened during the third act?
questions.answer: A storm knocked out the lights and the power.

questions.question: How did Marguerite help the Dame at the end?
questions.answer: She quietly supplied the forgotten line from the wings.

questions.question: What did the Dame decide after the performance?
questions.answer: To retire in the spring and let Marguerite take over.
